lessons.title: Greetings
lessons.intro: Italians greet each other warmly and expect a bit of small talk before getting down to business — a rushed greeting can come across as cold.
lessons.didYouKnow: The double cheek kiss ("il bacio") between friends starts on the LEFT cheek first in most of Italy — going right first is an easy tourist tell.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight into a request or question without any greeting first — even a quick "Buongiorno" before asking a shopkeeper something goes a long way.

quiz.question: In the traditional Italian cheek kiss, which side do you start on?
options: You don't kiss cheeks in Italy

lessons.title: Emergency Phrases
lessons.intro: You'll probably never need these — but having them ready before you land, rather than looking them up mid-emergency, is worth the three minutes.
lessons.didYouKnow: Italy's single emergency number is 112 (it routes to police, ambulance, or fire depending on what you say) — it works across the whole EU, not just Italy.
commonMistakes: Assuming your home country's emergency number works — in Italy (and the whole EU) it's 112, not 911.

quiz.question: What's the general emergency number in Italy?

lessons.title: Coffee Culture
lessons.intro: Coffee in Italy is a fast, standing-at-the-bar ritual with its own strict unwritten rules — very different from a sit-down coffee shop visit.
lessons.didYouKnow: Ordering a cappuccino after 11am is considered strange by most Italians — milky coffee is a breakfast drink only. After a meal, order an espresso instead.
commonMistakes: Ordering a cappuccino after a meal — Italians will notice, even if they're too polite to say anything.
Sitting down at a café table without checking the price list — table service usually costs 2-3x more than standing at the bar.

quiz.question: When do most Italians avoid drinking cappuccino?
Why might a coffee cost more than expected?
options: Sitting at a table has separate table service pricing
It doesn't — price is always the same

lessons.title: Ordering Food
lessons.intro: An Italian meal at a real restaurant unfolds in courses over a couple of hours — it's a relaxed social event, not a quick refuel.
lessons.didYouKnow: A "coperto" (cover charge) of a couple of euros per person is standard at most sit-down restaurants — it's not a scam, it covers bread and table service, and it'll be on the menu.
commonMistakes: Asking for extra cheese on a seafood pasta — traditionally considered a culinary mismatch, and some restaurants will visibly hesitate or decline.

quiz.question: What is the "coperto" on an Italian restaurant bill?

lessons.title: Train Etiquette
lessons.intro: Italy's train network is a great way to get around — but a couple of easy-to-miss rules can turn a cheap ticket into an on-the-spot fine.
lessons.didYouKnow: Paper regional tickets must be validated ("convalidare") at a small green or white machine on the platform before boarding — buying the ticket alone isn't enough, and conductors do check.

phrases.translation: Do I need to validate my ticket?

commonMistakes: Forgetting to validate a paper regional ticket before boarding — this is one of the most common (and avoidable) fines tourists get in Italy.

quiz.question: What must you do with most paper regional train tickets before boarding?
options: Validate them at a platform machine
Show them to a police officer

lessons.title: Tourist Mistakes
lessons.intro: A few small habits mark someone as a first-time visitor in Italy — none are a big deal, but avoiding them makes daily interactions smoother.
lessons.didYouKnow: Many historic town centers ("centro storico") are restricted-traffic zones (ZTL) monitored by cameras — driving into one without authorization results in an automatic fine by mail, sometimes months later.

phrases.translation: Where is the restricted traffic zone?

commonMistakes: Driving or even briefly stopping in a ZTL zone without checking signage first.
Wearing beachwear away from the beach — many churches and some restaurants will turn away visitors in shorts/tank tops.
Tipping heavily like in the US — a small rounding-up is appreciated, but large tips aren't the norm.

quiz.question: What is a ZTL zone?
options: A restricted-traffic zone monitored by cameras

quiz.question: Is heavy American-style tipping expected in Italy?
options: No, a small rounding-up is enough

lessons.title: Shopping Phrases
lessons.intro: Shopping in Italy ranges from small family-run boutiques to big-city department stores — the phrases below cover you in either.
lessons.didYouKnow: Many smaller shops still close for a few hours in the early afternoon ("riposo"), especially in smaller towns — a locked door at 2pm usually just means it reopens later.
commonMistakes: Showing up to a small shop right at 1-2pm expecting it to be open — check for posted riposo hours first.

quiz.question: What is "riposo"?
options: A midday closing period for small shops

lessons.title: Regional Expressions
lessons.intro: Standard Italian is understood everywhere, but you'll hear plenty of regional flavor depending where you are — a few of these will help you follow along.
lessons.didYouKnow: "Boh" is an extremely common, almost universal Italian expression of "I don't know / I have no idea," usually said with a shrug — you'll hear it constantly once you notice it.
commonMistakes: Assuming textbook Italian phrases will sound natural everywhere — plenty of daily conversation leans on casual expressions like these instead.

lessons.title: Scam Awareness
lessons.intro: Italy is generally very safe, but popular tourist areas do attract a handful of well-known, low-stakes scams worth knowing about in advance.
lessons.didYouKnow: The "friendship bracelet" scam near major landmarks — someone ties a bracelet on your wrist while distracting you, then demands payment — is common enough that most locals will just tell you to keep walking.
commonMistakes: Stopping to engage with strangers offering "free" bracelets, roses, or petitions near major landmarks — a firm "No, grazie" and continuing to walk is the normal, expected response.
Not checking that a taxi's meter is running before the ride starts.

quiz.question: What's the best response to a stranger trying to tie a "free" bracelet on you near a landmark?
options: Let them, then negotiate the price
Give them your bag to hold
Follow them to their friend's shop
